text: src/store/searchIndex.test.ts times indexOrder and rows() against wall-clock bounds (100 ms, 50 ms), which fail when the machine is loaded

Asked: found 15:16 (not asked): the Stop hook's suite ran beside three whole Helium verdicts and read 261.6 ms against the test's 100 ms; then, asked: 'Add that to F3's detail. Also, do we have other tests that are effectively performance tests? I'm not sure this test makes sense, and I'm also not sure a cut-off of 100ms is sensible. Plus currently it's 17,365 entries, so the 13,600 number is no longer relevant either. I'm wondering what the underlying reason for this test was.' WHAT FAILS: only the stopwatch. The test (searchIndex.test.ts:50-66) builds 13,600 keys, times one indexOrder call with performance.now() and requires under 100 ms, then times a second rows() call and requires under 50 ms; the ordering itself came out right. Quiet, the call takes 6-9 ms (MEASURED, 5 runs, 2026-11-23); loaded, 261.6 ms. WHY IT EXISTS: the phase 3 review (2026-09-08, e8b4781; conversion plan's record, lines 1371-1374) measured indexOrder at 500-708 ms a call over 13,600 keys, the journal's size then, paid on every search scan, because it filtered every key once per day; the fix made it one bucketed pass and kept the order while the key set stands, and the test pinned that under 100 ms. Its purpose is to stop the per-day filter shape coming back, not a time. THE OTHERS: this is the only test in src/, tools/ and one-offs/ with wall-clock bounds (io.test's 30 s timeout is a ceiling for a big zip, not a measure). THE SIZE: the backup holds 17,363 .md entries today (MEASURED). THE WAY OUT: check the shape, not the time: count indexOrder's comparisons (or the keys each pass visits) and require about one pass over the keys, and count that a second rows() does not order again, as the test above it counts flattens (expect(flattens).toBe(10)); the key count then matters only as a size, and the reader decides whether to keep it at a journal's size. Done when: the reader decides between that, a bound that measures the code, or dropping the bounds; then built test-first (a src/ test change, so an accept).

note: closed as asked: the timed test is deleted, not reworked. It was the phase 3 review's forcing function for the one-pass ordering (500-708 ms a call over 13,600 keys before it, 6-9 ms now); its wall-clock bounds read the machine's load, not the code. The ordering stays checked by the test above it, and searchIndex.ts keeps the review's measurement as the reason for the one pass, unpinned.
